alt: Top: an EVS modelled as a system, with inputs such as upbringing, culture and media, processing by values and beliefs, and outputs such as decisions, votes and purchases. Bottom: the spectrum from ecocentric through anthropocentric to technocentric, with the solar-farm stakeholders placed: a local group (ecocentric), a farmer (anthropocentric) and an engineer (technocentric).
caption: Place a stakeholder on the spectrum using evidence from what they say.

alt: Systems diagram of fictional Lake Varn storing 1200 million cubic metres. Inputs: river inflow 310, rain 45 and groundwater 25. Outputs: river outflow 290, evaporation 70 (a transformation) and abstraction 35. Inputs total 380 and outputs 395, so the lake loses 15 a year, 1.25% of its storage.
caption: When outputs exceed inputs, the storage shrinks: the system is not in steady state.

alt: Three systems with dashed boundaries. In an open system, such as most ecosystems, both energy and matter cross the boundary. In a closed system, close to Earth as a whole, energy crosses but matter does not. In an isolated system neither crosses, and no natural example exists.
caption: What crosses the boundary, energy, matter or neither, defines the type of system.

alt: Four small graphs over time. Steady-state: the line fluctuates around an average. Static: a flat line with no change. Stable: after a disturbance the system returns to its old level. Unstable: after a disturbance it settles at a new level. Below, a tipping point is defined as a threshold past which a small change causes a large, lasting shift.
caption: Living systems are in steady state; stable systems return after disturbance, unstable ones do not.

alt: A community woodland holds 48 000 cubic metres of timber. Natural income, 3.5% growth, adds 1680 a year while 2100 is harvested, 125% of income, so the stock falls to 47 580 after one year. The largest sustainable harvest is 1680.
caption: A harvest is sustainable only if it does not exceed natural income.

alt: Bar chart for fictional Country P: ecological footprint 4.8 global hectares per person against biocapacity 2.0, a deficit of 2.8 per person. The footprint is 2.4 times biocapacity, and with 12 million people the total deficit is 33.6 million gha.
caption: A footprint larger than biocapacity means an ecological deficit.

alt: Left: the doughnut, with an inner social foundation ring, an outer ecological ceiling based on planetary boundaries, and the safe and just space between them. Right: the linear take, make, throw away model compared with a circular economy that designs out waste, keeps products and materials in use and regenerates natural systems.
caption: Aim for the safe and just space, and close the loop on materials.

alt: Six stages in order: a baseline study of the site, prediction of likely impacts, mitigation measures, a report with a non-technical summary, a decision, and monitoring after the project starts. A note lists limits: uncertain predictions, short-term baseline data and decisions that may still favour economic gain.
caption: An EIA runs from a baseline study before approval to monitoring afterwards.
